ideas.hypothesis: Chinese prefectures with larger increases in imported machinery see larger rises in both the local college share and the local college wage premium. A substantial part of the measured premium rise comes from high-ability graduates choosing to move into machinery-importing prefectures (Roy-type selection), so the effect on the premium is smaller for stayers than for migrants.
ideas.test: Use prefecture-level census microdata (2000, 2005 1% survey, 2010) linked to customs data on machinery imports by prefecture, with a shift-share instrument built from initial industry mix and national import growth. Estimate effects on college share and on the college premium, separately for natives/stayers and in-migrants, and with and without a Dahl/Lee-style selection correction based on migration probabilities.
ideas.disconfirming: The premium effect is just as large for stayers as for migrants and does not shrink after the selection correction, or machinery imports show no association with the local premium at all.

ideas.hypothesis: Exogenous falls in expected adult survival (the 1918 Spanish flu) lower schooling investment by cohorts of school age, and this effect is larger where property rights are weakly protected, because longer horizons pay off only when returns to human capital are secure.
ideas.test: Build a cross-country (or Italian regional) panel of school enrollment and cohort years of schooling for 1900-1960, linked to 1918-19 flu excess mortality and to historical indicators of institutional quality and democracy. Run cohort difference-in-differences comparing cohorts exposed versus not exposed at school age, with an interaction for institutional quality.
ideas.disconfirming: Cohorts exposed to high flu mortality show no drop in schooling, or the drop is no larger in places with weak institutions.

ideas.hypothesis: Income-based human capital stock indices (Mulligan and Sala-i-Martin style) that weight attainment groups by observed education wage premia overstate stock growth, because part of the premium reflects degree (sheepskin) effects and ability composition rather than skills. Indices built from ability- and degree-adjusted returns grow more slowly.
ideas.test: Using Korean labour force microdata (or NLSY79 plus CPS for the US), estimate returns by attainment with and without separating years of schooling from degree receipt and with ability controls (test scores). Build the stock index both ways for 1980-2010 and compare growth rates and growth-accounting shares.
ideas.disconfirming: The adjusted and unadjusted indices grow at nearly the same rate (within a few percent), showing that degree and composition effects do not distort income-based stock measures.

ideas.hypothesis: College graduates who chose their field for investment reasons (expected earnings and employment) are less likely to be both vertically and horizontally mismatched early in their careers. Among those who are mismatched, they are more likely to change jobs in order to correct the mismatch than graduates who chose for consumption or social-norm reasons.
ideas.test: Use the Korean Graduates Occupational Mobility Survey panel, coding reported reasons for choosing the major into investment versus consumption/norm motives. Estimate multinomial models of mismatch type (vertical only, horizontal only, both) and hazard models of job change conditional on mismatch, with controls for institution, field and gender.
ideas.disconfirming: Investment-motivated graduates are mismatched no less often, or their job-mobility response to mismatch is no stronger than that of other graduates.

ideas.hypothesis: Growth-accounting estimates of human capital's contribution to growth in China and India depend on whether skill premia are treated as reflecting workers' skills or local technology. Letting province-level returns to skill vary with technology and institutional indicators sharply reduces the share of output variation attributed to human capital stock.
ideas.test: Using Chinese provincial (or Indian state) data on attainment, province-specific Mincerian returns from household surveys (CHNS/CHIP or NSS) and output per worker, carry out development accounting under (i) a common return and (ii) returns allowed to depend on technology proxies such as FDI, R&D or the capital-skill ratio. Compare the variance shares attributed to human capital.
ideas.disconfirming: The human capital share of cross-province output variation is essentially unchanged across the two specifications.

ideas.hypothesis: In economies still in a physical-capital-driven stage of growth, a higher aggregate saving rate predicts faster later growth in average years of schooling, because capital deepening raises the return to skills. The link weakens once average schooling passes a threshold at which human capital becomes the main engine of growth.
ideas.test: Build an annual panel of East and Southeast Asian economies (including Thailand) for 1970-2010 with saving rates, capital stock series and average years of schooling for ages 25-64. Regress five-year growth in schooling on lagged saving rates and capital deepening, allowing a threshold in initial schooling (threshold regression).
ideas.disconfirming: Lagged saving rates do not predict schooling growth once income is controlled, or the relationship does not change across schooling levels.

ideas.hypothesis: Higher local private returns to secondary schooling raise children's primary completion, because they increase the option value of finishing primary school. Children in districts where secondary schooling pays more have lower primary dropout rates.
ideas.test: Using Albania LSMS waves (2002, 2005, 2008), estimate district-level returns to secondary schooling from adult wage equations. Then regress primary completion and dropout of children aged 10-15 on lagged district returns, with household controls and district fixed effects across waves.
ideas.disconfirming: District returns to secondary schooling are unrelated to primary completion, or are negatively related to it.

ideas.hypothesis: When the wage premium for low-level qualifications collapses (for example, the GCSE premium among young UK workers), the gaps between low-qualified and unqualified workers in non-wage outcomes (employer training, job satisfaction, employment stability) persist. Wage-based measures therefore understate the human capital returns at the bottom of the education distribution.
ideas.test: Using BHPS 1991-2008 linked to Understanding Society, estimate by cohort the returns to GCSE-level qualifications (compared with none) for wages, receipt of employer-provided training, job satisfaction and months employed. Use the same controls across cohorts and compare trends across outcomes.
ideas.disconfirming: The non-wage gaps shrink in step with the wage premium and reach zero at the same time.

ideas.hypothesis: In Brazil, Russia, India and China, primary enrollment is linked to ICT diffusion and growth only through later progression to secondary schooling. Once secondary enrollment is controlled, primary enrollment has no independent association, and this holds across alternative education datasets.
ideas.test: Build a 1975-2015 panel of BRIC countries plus comparison emerging economies with internet and mobile subscriptions per capita and GDP per worker. Measure education with World Bank enrollment, Barro-Lee attainment and Cohen-Soto data. Estimate panel models with country fixed effects, with and without secondary enrollment as a control, and check consistency across datasets.
ideas.disconfirming: Primary enrollment keeps a significant independent association with ICT diffusion or growth after controlling for secondary enrollment, consistently across datasets.

ideas.hypothesis: In emerging economies, Granger causality from secondary-education expansion to GDP growth appears or strengthens only after market deregulation or a shift toward advanced-technology policy, because those reforms raise demand for secondary-level skills.
ideas.test: Using annual data for 1970-2015 on secondary enrollment and real GDP for Nigeria, Brazil, India and China, identify reform dates (deregulation and technology-policy programs). Run Toda-Yamamoto causality tests in pre- and post-reform subsamples, and in a panel with a reform interaction, checking robustness to endogenous break tests.
ideas.disconfirming: The direction and strength of causality from secondary education to GDP are the same before and after reforms, or causality runs only from GDP to enrollment.
